11062-the-dozen-from-lakerim:
Rupert Hughes wrote this 1899 school story about twelve boys at an academy in the invented town of Lakerim. The Lakerim Athletic Club, well known to townsfolk, faces a blow when Father Time blots out work the boys took pains with, leaving them blue. Hughes apologises for saying little about books and studies, sticking instead to games and gambols between classes.

Illustrations show a cross-country run, a boxing match, boys tied in sacks, a train stopped for Kingston, and books burning. A cold wave from the west freezes the town, stoves need coaxing, and professors scamper on slippery paths. Hughes writes boy life with humour and warmth, and the book, half first printed in St. Nicholas, remains a lively picture of preparatory school sport and friendship.
13004-more-goops-and-how-not-to-be-them-:
Gelett Burgess wrote More Goops and How Not to Be Them as a manners manual for impolite infants, with ninety illustrations by the author. Goops, rude children who tilt chairs and bite awful mouthfuls, teach by bad example. Rhymes teach soup manners: push the spoon away like little boats to sea, and unload from the side like ships. Baby's Apology and other verses follow.

The book, a sequel to Goops and How to Be Them, mixes nonsense verse with practical lessons on eating, sitting, and speaking politely. Burgess's drawings make the rude behaviour funny rather than scolding. The volume charms readers of children's nonsense and manners books.
14532-the-honorable-peter-stirling-and-w:
Paul Leicester Ford's 1894 novel follows Peter Stirling, a solid, sensible young lawyer who rises in New York politics without losing his honesty. The title points to reputation: what people thought of him shaped his career.

Peter dines with judges and society ladies, argues cases, and endures the talk of Mrs. Purple's circle, while friends note his lack of polish and his steady character. Ford writes with humor about ward politics, dinner parties, and reform. The novel is a thoughtful study of integrity in public life, and it was among the best political novels of its decade.
1544-the-passionate-pilgrim:
The Passionate Pilgrim is a small collection of love poems and sonnets published under Shakespeare's name in 1599, though only some are certainly his. It opens with a sonnet on lovers who knowingly believe each other's lies, and moves through complaints, praise, and parting in varied moods.

Short, musical, and varied, the pieces show the Elizabethan love lyric in many moods, from playful to bitter. Scholars still sort the true Shakespeare from imitations. The book is a slight but charming relic of Shakespeare's age, best read as a sampler of the era's love poetry.
15693-t-de-witt-talmage-as-i-knew-him:
A memoir of the famous American preacher T. De Witt Talmage, begun by Talmage himself and finished by his wife. E. P. Dutton and Company issued the book in New York in 1912, with pictures. Talmage tells his life in milestones, from youth to fame in Brooklyn pulpits. His widow adds closing chapters on his last years.

The milestones trace preaching, travel, church building, and meetings with notable men of the age. Talmage's voice stays warm and plain, full of anecdotes from the pulpit and the road. His wife's chapters give the home side of a public life. Together they form a portrait of a preacher who filled halls and reached readers through print, sermons, and sheer presence.
16334-sundown-slim:
Sundown Slim opens with its hero riding west from Albuquerque in the un-upholstered privacy of a box car, only to wake at Antelope, Arizona, as the freight rumbles on across the mesas. Annoyed at negligent service, Slim rolls and cords his blankets, meaning to leave the car to the base uses of corporate greed and a shipper of baled hay. He finds the door locked since he took possession, hammers on it, and trades compliments with an unseen rescuer.

The door slides back and Slim leaps out to meet, not a bucolic station agent, but a belted and booted figure of another sort. From that comic arrival grows a Western tale of drifters, ranches, and trouble. Readers who like light, good-humored cowboy fiction will enjoy Slim's adventures.
18388-robert-burns-how-to-know-him:
William Allan Neilson, professor of English at Harvard, wrote this 1917 guide to Robert Burns, with a portrait of the poet. Neilson, author of Essentials of Poetry, published the book with Bobbs-Merrill at Indianapolis. The volume pairs a life of Burns with readings of his poems, so a new reader can meet the man and his work together.

Chapters trace Burns from Alloway, Mount Oliphant, and Lochlea, through Mossgiel, Edinburgh, Ellisland, and Dumfries. Later chapters treat his inheritance of language and literature, Burns and Scottish song, satires and epistles, and descriptive and narrative poetry. A list of poems runs from Address to the Deil and Ae Fond Kiss to Afton Water. Readers get Burns made approachable: life, Scots tongue, song, and satire in one clear volume.
2005-piccadilly-jim:
P. G. Wodehouse's Piccadilly Jim follows Jimmy Crocker, a young American in London known as Piccadilly Jim, whose pranks and scrapes keep his family in despair. Jim's father wants him settled, his aunt wants him married. Jim wants only his freedom, until a girl and a plot involving a kidnapped boy change his mind.

Wodehouse writes the farce with his usual lightness, and the novel's complications — mistaken identities, a stolen child, and a romance conducted through jokes — resolve in the happiest possible way. The book is a classic of Wodehouse's early manner, and its hero's charm carries a plot that never quite stands still.
23119-a-forgotten-hero-or-not-for-him:
Clarice dresses with care in A Forgotten Hero, or Not for Him. Clarice wears her dark hair brushed smooth and curled up all around, cut short enough for the style. Her gown is long and loose in the Princess fashion, its train tucked under one arm as she walks.

Fashion detail like this carries the social world of the tale, where a forgotten hero's worth must be weighed against appearances. The double title poses the heroine's question, is the overlooked man for her, or not? Domestic fiction of the period loved that weighing. Dress, visits, and small slights build the scales. Readers get a quiet courtship problem, dressed in Princess style and judged by character in the end.
24458-still-jim:
Honore Willsie published this novel in 1915, after serial publication, under the title Still Jim. It follows Jim, a boy of the small town of Exham, from his childhood swimming hole. That pine-grove pool was a boy sanctuary, too shallow for men. Jim grows into a young engineer working on roads and dams in the desert country.

Later chapters follow Jim's work with foremen and road crews, his friendship with Pen, and his courtship of Sara. He learns to lead men and to hold his own against rivals. Willsie blends small-town boyhood, desert landscape, and the building of the West into a warm story of character, work, and steady love.
24634-reminiscences-of-the-military-life:
Charles Hersey wrote these reminiscences of Colonel Timothy Bigelow, commander of the Fifteenth Regiment of the Massachusetts Line in the Continental Army during the War of the Revolution. The book was printed at Worcester in 1860. Its contents run from a monument to Bigelow through early efforts for liberty.

Later chapters follow the minute men, Bigelow as a prisoner, service in Pennsylvania, and the winter at Valley Forge. Hersey gathers memory, record, and tribute into a short life of a Massachusetts officer. Readers of Revolutionary history will find it a useful and affectionate portrait.
25810-in-connection-with-the-de-willough:
Frances Hodgson Burnett writes In Connection with the De Willoughby Claim. It appeared in a special limited edition from the American News Company in 1899. It sold at fifty cents in paper covers. Scribner's Sons held copyright, sanctioning this paper edition but not rebinding for sale.

High noon at Talbot's Cross-roads, mercury at ninety-eight in the shade, opens the tale. Before the war, no people stood better known or more praised than the De Willoughbys. Burnett says so at the start. The claim that follows turns on family, property, and southern honour in a short novel of inheritance and pride.
26953-jessie-carlton-the-story-of-a-girl:
Francis Forrester's 1861 children's tale, one of the Glen Morris Stories, tells of Jessie Carlton, a girl who fought with Little Impulse, the Wizard, and conquered him. The book's note to parents states its aim plainly: to plant pure, noble character in children through living characters rather than prosy precepts.

Jessie's victories come chapter by chapter, against cousins, the wizard in the field, and Madge Clifton, with a skating party along the way. The story charms while it teaches, leading young readers to abhor the false and love the right, in the earnest Sunday-school style of its day.
27174-captain-jim:
Mary Grant Bruce's Captain Jim, published by Ward, Lock in 1919, opens with Jim and Wally on little green chairs in Hyde Park, watching red motor-buses rock away from Hyde Park Corner. The chapters run from John O'Neill's legacy and the home for tired people to settling in at Homewood.

Norah, practicing putts on the terrace, meets a short, strongly built captain with three stars asking after Homewood. Kidnapping, assorted guests, Australia in Surrey, and the watch on the Rhine follow, in a wartime story of a house that takes in the tired and gives them work.
27234-my-father-as-i-recall-him:
Mamie Dickens's My Father as I Recall Him, from the Roxburghe Press, remembers Charles Dickens through his eldest daughter's eyes. The book's sad note explains that Mamie's sister died before the proofs, in type and ready for correction, could be submitted to her for revision.

Chapters recall seeing Gad's Hill as a child, his domestic side and home love, his love of children, neatness, and punctuality, and the original of Little Nell. Later chapters cover Christmas at Gad's Hill, his work rooms, his writing hours, Nicholas Nickleby, Pickwick and Boz, and the death of Thackeray.
27453-colorado-jim:
George Goodchild published this western novel with A. L. Burt in New York in 1922, by arrangement with W. J. Watt and Company. Its hero Jim begins as a son of the West. Chapters carry him through bright lights, social advancement, Angela, frost and fire, a great awakening, and a climax on the white trail.

The book opens at dawn over the Medicine Bow range, where a band of blood-red light breaks along the serried edge and the whole range flames up as the sun rises. Later chapters bring high stakes, fruitless toil, the wilderness, the terror of the North, a great lie, and gold. Goodchild writes a full-blooded adventure of the West and its fortunes.
28361-british-socialism-an-examination-o:
J. Ellis Barker's British Socialism, published in 1908, examines socialist doctrines, policy, aims, and practical proposals in Britain, chapter by chapter. Barker begins by asking what socialism means, then works through socialist views on capital, taxation, the empire, foreign policy, the army, and the monarchy.

Later chapters take up parliament, local government, agriculture, railways, banking, free trade, education, thrift, law, women and the family, Christianity, communism, and anarchism. Barker closes by judging how far socialism had grown, how its advance might be checked, and whether a socialist state could work at all. The book is a detailed snapshot of Edwardian political debate.
28770-the-story-of-tim:
George Borrow translated this short Russian tale, The Story of Tim, printed for private circulation in London in 1913 from a Thomas J. Wise pamphlet. Timoney, called Tim, is a sharp lad who has learned nothing but to play the fife. His old parents, one nearly bald from his fur cap and one humped, argue over his future trade.

The father favors blacksmith or tailor, while the mother rejects both: the smith looks like a devil in fire and soot, and the tailor's doubled-up sitting brings on consumption. She wants a goldsmith or painter instead, though the fees would swallow all they own. The dispute nearly comes to blows. Readers get a droll folk tale in Borrow's plain, lively English, with a family quarrel at its heart.
32195-the-battle-of-blenheim:
Hilaire Belloc's The Battle of Blenheim, published in London by Stephen Swift and Company in 1911, is a short, map-driven battle history. Its five parts run from The Political Objective and The Early War through The March to the Danube and The Seven Weeks, the Three Phases, to The Action. A frontispiece plate shows the battle, and maps trace Marlborough's march beyond the hills separating the Rhine from the Danube.

Other maps show Marlborough and Baden marching across Marcin's front from Ulm to Donauworth. Donauworth appears as the key of Bavaria from the north-west, and Eugene's Danube march comes out of the Black Forest. A final map shows the situation when Eugene reached Hochstadt in early August 1704. Readers get a compact account of Blenheim, where politics, marching, and battle are laid out in maps and clear prose.
35555-kim:
Rudyard Kipling wrote Kim, with rights pages dated nineteen hundred and nineteen hundred and one. A long list of Kipling's books stands in front, from The Jungle Book to Stalky and Company. The tale opens in Lahore, in India.

Kim sits astride the gun Zam-Zammah, on her brick platform by the Lahore Museum. The natives call that museum the Wonder House. Who holds Zam-Zammah, the saying runs, holds the Punjab. The great green-bronze gun is the first loot of each conqueror of the land. Verse heads the first chapter, on those who tread the narrow way. Kim, an Irish orphan raised in the bazaars, stands at the tale's centre.
41380-the-history-of-burke-and-hare-and-:
George Mac Gregor wrote a history of Burke and Hare that came out at Glasgow in 1884. Mac Gregor had also written a history of Glasgow. His book calls itself a scrap from the crime rolls of Scotland. Seven plates show scenes and faces from the case.

Burke and Hare killed folk and sold the dead to men of science for study. Mac Gregor sets their crimes in the wider trade in stolen corpses of that age. He sought to give the first full, linked tale of the case in time order. The tale runs to the Anatomy Act of 1832. That act made grave theft needless, and the book shows why the law had to change.
41988-let-us-follow-him:
Let Us Follow Him is a religious tale by Henryk Sienkiewicz, translated from the Polish by Jeremiah Curtin. Little, Brown of Boston printed it in 1897. A publishers' note explains the separate volume. The story, though included in the collection Hania, deserved its own issue for one reason. It gave Sienkiewicz the idea of writing Quo Vadis.

The period is that of the death of Christ. Antea, the wife of a Roman patrician, is ill with terrible visions. A physician advises her to seek the air of Jerusalem. There she and her husband meet Pilate, who tells them of the doctrine of the Nazarene. Around that meeting Sienkiewicz builds a small, fervent drama of a pagan soul at the foot of the cross. Curtin's translation carried it to the English world at the height of the Quo Vadis sensation.
42690-the-mesmerist-s-victim:
Alexandre Dumas wrote a historical romance here in translation by Henry Llewellyn Williams, issued at New York in 1892 in a cheap subscription series. Its double title names Andrea de Taverney as the mesmerist's victim. Dumas's Monte Cristo and Three Musketeers series are paraded on the title page as his credentials.

The edition is a railway-age reprint, priced at twenty-five cents, with a house-plans advertisement bound in front of the title. Mesmerism, the magnetic craze of the old regime's last years, drives the plot's engine. Court intrigue and a victim caught in a stronger will's web are the promised fare. The translation follows the latest Paris edition, the title page says.
42875-wagner-as-i-knew-him:
Ferdinand Praeger wrote this portrait of Richard Wagner from long friendship. Longmans, Green printed the book in New York in 1892. Praeger gives it to the Earl of Dysart, a Wagner society head. He claims near half a century of close, frank friendship.

Praeger says Wagner bared his aims and his mind to him often. He will not defend Wagner in all things, he states plainly. Wagner had failings, and they will be dealt with without fear. The aim is an honest view of the great man and his motives. The writer knew Wagner as a friend over long years.
44079-sudden-jim:
Clarence Kelland wrote this tale of Sudden Jim and clothespin trade. Burt printed it in New York, Harper copyright 1916. Chapter one insists clothespins are made by art and machinery. No clothespin fields, no Clothespin Jimmy, the tale argues with humor.

James Ashe signed checks in marks few could read as his name. At sixty five, hale and hearty, he felt ripe for play. Fifty years hard labor stood as his served sentence in trade. He called his son James home, who disliked the clothespin business. The front plate shows Jim waving a flag of truce to Miss Ducharme in fun.
44400-ticktock-and-jim:
Keith Robertson wrote a boys horse book printed at Philadelphia and Toronto in 1948, with pictures by Wesley Dennis. The book is given to Christina, who at two is somewhat mixed up about horses and thinks they say moo. The trade opens the tale. Someone has to stay home to give Colonel Flesher that Jersey cow, the first page runs.

The reception, the first victory, new allies, and the pony express follow. The saddle, Horace, exile, and the lost horse fill the middle. Ticktock disappears, the conspirators meet, and Jean's ride leads to the mystery solved. The fire, a long night, and the recovery close the book. Jim felt proud that his father called him a man, the text shows, though it did not make up for missing the trip. A boy and a pony carry the story.
44433-jaufry-the-knight-and-the-fair-bru:
Mary Lafon wrote this tale of King Arthur's times, and Alfred Elwes turned it into English from the French. Addey and Co brought it out in 1856 with twenty plates by Gustave Dore. Its hero is Jaufry, a knight of the Round Table, and its lady is the fair Brunissende.

The plate list gives a taste of the plot: a king hangs helpless from a monster's horns. Jaufry speaks to a slain knight whose killer he does not know. Knights, burghers, minstrels, and jugglers crowd one feast scene. Wounds, a bleeding hero borne back by his troop, and a gloomy wood fill other plates. Young readers of 1856 got a full Arthurian romance in French dress.
45928-secrets-of-the-late-rebellion-now-:
Freese wrote Secrets of the Late Rebellion, Now Revealed for the First Time, at Philadelphia in 1882. Crombargar and Company put out the book. Freese says his aim is not a full war history. He deals in close, fresh facts that had not seen print, since most of the men in them were gone. Old facts serve as frame and cloth, while new facts form the scenes. He claims each tale can be trusted.

One long part runs the land blockade, with King Cotton at its heart. Freese tracks acts of the Confederate Congress and words from Presidents Davis and Lincoln. Later parts show secret routes and posts set up to pass men and news between North and South. The book gives a back-stairs view of the Civil War.
47068-the-growth-of-the-english-constitu:
Edward A Freeman wrote The Growth of the English Constitution from the Earliest Times, here in a second edition from London in 1873. Freeman was a late Fellow of Trinity College, Oxford. His preface asks that the work be judged as lectures, not as a book. The core was two lectures given at Leeds and Bradford last January.

Freeman expanded the latter part of the second lecture into a third chapter, with notes. He grants that a popular lecture cannot treat everything or go to the bottom of its picks. His aim is to awaken real interest and send readers to proper sources. He points above all to Professor Stubbs and his documents on early English institutions. Mottoes from the coronation oath and Bracton head the title page.
48041-the-study-of-elementary-electricit:
Thomas M St John wrote The Study of Elementary Electricity and Magnetism by Experiment as a home text book. He issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred with his own name on the press line. Two hundred trials fill its pages. All use cheap gear a student can build at home.

St John tells the student to start at the start. Each step must be clear before the next begins. Base laws come first, and flashy uses come later. Cost held him back from dear shop gear, he says. Hints on how to make each tool run through the text. His past books taught boys to build their own kit. School and home labs both form the book’s true class room.
50553-buddy-jim:
Buddy Jim is a picture story book for small children by Elizabeth Gordon, with pictures by John Rae. It was published by the Volland Company of Joliet, Illinois, in 1922. The hosted copy is from the twenty-third edition, a sign of how well the book sold.

Verses open the tale. Buddy Jim and his family are going to the country, and his city playmates pity him. The country is just land and air and sky, they say, with no boys and no games. Jim does not want to say goodbye. His friends shout their parting orders: bring back a tame bull-frog, and a grey squirrel for a cage. Left alone on the porch swing, Jim counts the joys he is leaving. Baseball, swimming in the lake, and the school gardens all plead against the trip. Daddy is indoors packing for an early start by motor car.
51864-tales-traditions-and-romance-of-bo:
Edward Ellis wrote tales, traditions, and romance of border and Revolutionary times, entered for copyright at New York in 1864 by a great house of cheap fiction. The preface promises a rare combination: the volume is almost strictly historical, yet as marvellous as the most romantic fiction, its sketches all authenticated.

Two classes fill it, incidents of the Revolution and of the frontier, with the customs of the Indians and the privations of the early settlers. Boys will find examples worthy of emulation, the preface says, and girls may gain dignity contemplating the devotion of the women of those days. The banks of the Ohio and the Muskingum, it prophesies, will one day be trodden as reverently as the storied Rhine.
53075-songs-of-the-glens-of-antrim:
Moira O'Neill wrote these Songs of the Glens of Antrim, here in an eleventh impression printed in New York in 1904. In her preface O'Neill says the songs were written by a Glenswoman in the dialect of the Glens. They were made chiefly for the pleasure of other Glens folk. The songs first came out in Blackwood and the Spectator, by leave of their editors.

The contents list songs of Glen Dun and Glenann, Corrymeela, and the Fairy Lough. Marriage, sea wrack, a grand match, and a sailor man stand among the themes. The first song sets gold on the whin-bush and the Fairy Thorn in flower, while the singer's love is far away. Longing for Ireland runs through the set, in plain dialect verse.
53308-historical-record-of-the-eighteent:
Richard Cannon compiled the Historical Record of the Eighteenth, or Royal Irish Regiment of Foot, printed in London in 1848, covering formation in 1684 and services to 1848. Cannon worked at the Adjutant-General's office at Horse Guards. General orders of January 1836 from King William command published accounts of every regiment's services in the British Army.

Each record must give formation, stations, battles, sieges, achievements, and colours or trophies captured from the enemy. The Royal Irish served across empire wars of the long eighteenth century and after in many stations. Cannon's series set the template for British regimental histories used by officers and families. Military historians get an official record in full detail.
53724-jessie-trim:
Farjeon wrote this novel for Tinsleys' Magazine, where it ran through the year 1874. Jessie Trim filled the first half in numbers from January to June, and the rest by December. Farjeon had written Blade-o'-Grass, Grif, and London's Heart by then.

My Grandmother's Wedding opens the tale, told by Jessie herself. I Am Frightened of My Shadow and My Grandmother's Long Stocking keep her young voice. Dark heads turn up fast: I Murder My Baby-Brother, and I Play the Part of Chief Mourner. A great change in her lot ends the part of the list shown here. Child eyes on a grown, hard world give the book its odd, sad charm.
55036-historical-record-of-the-sixteenth:
Richard Cannon compiled the Historical Record of the Sixteenth, or Bedfordshire, Regiment of Foot, printed by authority in London in MDCCCXLVIII. Cannon worked at the Adjutant General Office, Horse Guards. Plates aid the record. The account runs from the formation of the regiment in sixteen eighty eight through its services to eighteen forty eight. The series covers every regiment in Her Majesty service.

Contents march year by year, from formation and establishment to Stony Stratford quarters. The regiment embarked for Holland in sixteen eighty nine and engaged at Walcourt. Bruges, Brussels, and South Brabant follow. At Steenkirk in sixteen ninety two Colonel Hodges was killed. Landen, Dendermond, and later campaigns fill the record. Army historians get an official regimental history, dry and exact.
56837-historical-record-of-the-fifty-thi:
Richard Cannon compiled this record of the Fifty-Third (Shropshire) Regiment of Foot at the Adjutant-General's Office in London, and it was published in 1849. The history runs from the regiment's formation in 1755 through its services down to 1848. Its battle honours name Nieuport in October 1793, Tournay in May 1794, and Saint Lucia in May 1796, then the Peninsula battles of Talavera, Salamanca, Vittoria, the Pyrenees, Nivelle, and Toulouse.

The last honours listed are Aliwal and Sobraon, won in India on 28 January and 10 February 1846. Cannon's records follow a fixed plan: stations, campaigns, officers, and losses, set down plainly from official papers. Regimental histories of this kind were made as much for the corps itself as for the public. They gave soldiers a printed roll of what their regiment had done and where it had served.
57395-interim:
Dorothy M Richardson wrote Interim, first issued at London in 1919. The novel forms one part of a long series that holds Pointed Roofs, Backwater, Honeycomb, and The Tunnel. Deadlock was still in hand when Interim came out. Miriam Henderson stands at the heart of the tale.

Miriam comes late and wet to a house in the suburbs. Florrie meets her at the door with her bag in hand. Grace and Mrs Philps draw her in to the fire and to supper. Talk, small slights, and close thought fill the scene. Richardson stays close to Miriam's mind as she hears and weighs each word. The style is slow, close, and rich in small detail.
58377-a-short-list-of-scientific-books-p:
A Short List of Scientific Books is the trade catalogue of Spon Limited, of 57 Haymarket, London, sole English agents also for two New York houses. Its contents page sorts the stock by subject across some forty headings, from agriculture and architecture to telegraph codes, useful tables, and water supply.

Each entry gives a book's author, its count of illustrations and pages, its format, its place and year, and its price in shillings. Agriculture opens the list with a practical treatise on hemp culture for seed and fibre, a farm drainage manual, and talks on manures. A handbook on sugar for planters and refiners runs to 876 pages with 236 illustrations. Architecture and building follow with works on the Turkish bath and hydropathic establishments, and the catalogue continues through engineering, chemistry, mining, and workshop practice.
58489-a-short-list-of-scientific-books-p:
A Short List of Scientific Books is a publisher's catalogue from Spon Limited. Spon of Haymarket, London, issued the short list in June 1913. The firm stood as English agents for Clark and Spon and Chamberlain of New York. Prices in the catalogue apply to sales in the United Kingdom only. All books stand bound in cloth unless the list states otherwise.

Subjects run in letter order from agriculture to workshop practice inside. Architecture, artillery, aviation, and bridges fill the early pages listed. Cement and concrete, civil engineering, and curve tables follow next. Electrical engineering takes a long stretch of the catalogue's middle pages. Gas and oil engines, horology, hydraulics, and irrigation stand in turn. Logarithm tables, metallurgy, and mineralogy serve the working engineer reader. Railway engineering, sanitation, and water supply close the long list. A hemp treatise at two shillings sixpence opens the agriculture part.
63511-the-negro-laborer-a-word-to-him:
William Councill wrote a short word to Black laborers from Huntsville, Alabama, dated December 1887. Friends had asked him to speak in many towns on the labor question, and print lets him reach them all. Three texts from Genesis head the talk, on bread won by sweat and on the call to tame the earth.

Councill holds that work is ordained by God, and so it is a thing of honor, not shame. Work should have a plan and an aim, to build the earth up for the ease of all. A man who shuns work, he warns, harms the state, his kin, and his own soul.
6454-george-leatrim:
Susanna Moodie tells George Leatrim, subtitled The Mother's Test, through a lady friend's story of dishonesty in a relative branch of her family. At Westcliff, Dr. Leatrim preaches with eloquence, a principal attraction of the place, yet lives solitary, seldom in society, visiting only the poor or those needing spiritual advice. Since his wife and only son died, he has never been seen with a smile, though his sermons run full of warmth.

A mid passage counts the collection: one member put in ten, all the household, servants included, gave liberally, yet the box must have been robbed to a considerable amount. The uncle returns home miserable, for a great sin has been committed, and suspecting any household member feels almost as great a sin. Moodie writes a moral tale of theft, suspicion, and a mother's test of character.
64581-historical-record-of-the-twenty-se:
Historical Record of the Twenty-Second, or the Cheshire Regiment of Foot is an official regimental history compiled by Richard Cannon. Parker of London printed it in 1849, with plates. Cannon worked at the Adjutant-General's Office at Horse Guards. The volume accounts for the regiment from its formation in 1689 to 1849.

It belongs to the Historical Records of the British Army, a series begun by command of William the Fourth. The contents promise the standard parts: the period and circumstances of the regiment's formation, the stations where it has been employed, and its battles, sieges, and other services. Cannon's records were compiled from the regiment's own books under a general order of 1836. The Cheshire volume is dry, exact, and made to last: a regiment's memory bound by authority.
66221-turkey-the-great-powers-and-the-ba:
Edward Mead Earle, assistant professor of history at Columbia, studies the Bagdad Railway as a case of imperialism. Macmillan published the book in New York in 1923 and reprinted it in 1924. His frontispiece maps the Turkish railways in 1918.

Earle opens with an ancient trade route revived, then a backward Turkey inviting economic use of its natural wealth. German interest follows: the first rails, the traders, and at last the German government. The Sultan, he argues, mortgaged his empire in the conventions of 1899 and 1902 with the Anatolian Railways company. The locomotive was to supplant the camel, and the purse-strings loosened accordingly.
66621-historical-record-of-the-fifty-six:
Historical Record of the Fifty-Sixth, or the West Essex Regiment, stands in a series of regimental histories made under royal command. Richard Cannon compiled the series at the Adjutant-General's office, Horse Guards. General orders of January 1836 lay down what each record must hold.

Each account gives a regiment's raising, its stations, and its battles and sieges. It names the officers and men killed or wounded, with place and date. It also lists men honored with titles or medals for gallant conduct. The West Essex volume thus preserves one regiment's service in the form the army itself ordered kept, a sober roll of marches, fights, and losses.
66905-the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bie:
Ambrose Bierce fills volume eleven of his Collected Works, published in New York and Washington in 1912 under the title Antepenultimata. A publisher note explains that most of the volume had appeared in San Francisco as The Shadow on the Dial and Other Essays. Revisions and additions by the author mark this printing.

The essays open with The Shadow on the Dial itself, then turn to civilization, the game of politics, and a possible benefactor. Warlike America speaks for Bierce the old soldier, who had fought through the Civil War and never lost his suspicion of glory. Howes compiled and edited the San Francisco book, and the Neale house thanks him and the publisher Robertson for the loan of the matter. Bierce's essays are acid in essay dress: short, quotable, and aimed at cant.
67299-through-the-crater-s-rim:
Hyatt Verrill, who wrote Beyond the Pole, made this lost-world tale for the science fiction magazines. Through the Crater's Rim finds a strange race living in a dead volcano's bowl in Central America. The frame note backs the fancy with news.

Only a few years before, it says, science found a new race in Panama, the White Indians. So the tale's hidden folk strain belief no worse. A plate states the peril at full stretch: a vine coils round a dying man and drags him into the tree. A second vine crawls for the watcher, who leaps with a wild yell. Into the Unknown, chapter one is named, and Lieutenant Hazen swears the place is there.
67371-bokwala-the-story-of-a-congo-victi:
Bokwala: The Story of a Congo Victim was written by a Congo resident and printed at London by the Religious Tract Society in 1910. The preface is by Doctor Grattan Guinness. The tale is told in the first person by a Congolese man. It begins with his boyhood at home: how his people lived, worked and played. Their one fear was the cannibals.

The boy is captured by cannibals, made a slave, and escapes home over the river. He courts and marries. Then the white men come, first talking of one Jesus, then the trader Bokakala, who wants rubber. The chapters darken stage by stage. Rubber quotas, short weight at the market, a whipping at the palaver. Forest guards oppress the villages, women are enslaved, and punishments turn ghastly.
69968-frank-allen-at-gold-fork-or-locati:
Graham Forbes sends his boy hero west in Frank Allen at Gold Fork, or Locating the Lost Claim, from Garden City Publishing in 1926. Forbes had written Frank Allen and His Motor Boat and Frank Allen at Rockspur Ranch in the same series. A front plate shows a man snatching up a burning brand and hurling it through the air.

Chapter one opens at Rockspur Ranch, where Frank and Lanky Wallace spot a queer prowler in moonlight outside the house. They rule out old foes Nash Yesson and Lef Seller, and guess the stranger hunts a map they took with gold nuggets from a rusty iron chest. That map, left by Josh Kinney, holds clues to a long lost gold claim he once worked.
70397-how-to-swim: How to Swim is a handbook title in the Spalding Athletic Library, a long line of cheap sports guides. The opening pages in hand are the Spalding lists, not swim lessons. They name guides on base ball, golf, tennis, skating, and gym games, with prices and bound sets. One list names How to Swim and Competitive Diving as a bound mate to Speed Swimming. The lists date from late 1916 and show how wide the sports line ran.
71751-in-the-swim:
In the Swim is a novel of New York society by Richard Henry Savage. Rand, McNally published it at Chicago and New York in 1898. Its subtitle calls it a story of currents in gayest New York. The contents divide the tale into three books. A Rising Star forms the first book of the story. Young Lochinvar Has Come out of the West opens it. The Drift of a Day in New York City follows.

With the Current forms the second book of the tale. A plunger speculator's gay life is shown under the rose there. Miss Romaine Garland, stenographer, enters as a chapter title. On a Lee Shore forms the third and stormy book. Miss Marble's Waterloo and a wedding in high life fill it. In the Dark Waters closes the fifteen chapters. Savage mixes Wall Street plunging with society romance.
71775-the-prior-claim:
The Prior Claim, a novel by Eleanor Mercein Kelly, is billed as a gripping romance of Indian war and pioneer life in Kentucky. Pictures by L F Wilford go with the text. On the Elkhorn River near Frankfort, two rough stone chimneys in a cornfield mark the tale's ground. They are what is left of a log cabin built a century and more before.

The opening rebuilds that cabin in words. Ezra Todd and his groomsmen raised it for his bride Polly, with puncheon tables, a pole bed, a spinning wheel, and a hooded cradle. A musket stood in a rack behind a door studded with nails and pierced with peep holes. The scene sets a frontier home armed against sudden attack.
72273-as-many-as-touched-him:
As Many As Touched Him is a religious tale by Eglanton Thorne. The Religious Tract Society published it in London from Paternoster Row. The story opens on a bright July morning at a farmyard gate. Ellen Mansfield waits there for the country postman. She hopes for a letter and ignores her mother's call.

Ellen is sixteen, the eldest of ten children. She hates house-work and shirks it when she can. The chapter titles trace a harder road ahead. They promise Jerry's trial, the great Physician, and days in a work-room. Suffering for conscience sake and a stay in hospital follow. The last chapters jump ten years forward. Jerry's faith, one title promises, has its reward. The tale belongs to the tract society tradition of fiction with a Christian lesson at its heart.
72560-sink-or-swim:
Sink or Swim, a novel in three volumes by the author of Recommended to Mercy, came from Tinsley Brothers of London in 1868. The first chapter, What They Said in the Village, opens over tea in the shop of the widow Thwaytes at Switcham. There the gossips deplore that John Beacham means to marry Honor Blake, an Irishwoman.

Her friend the widow Tamfrey, a monthly nurse with an only daughter put out to service, shares the talk. The village sits less than an hour and a half by express train from London, yet keeps its old ways. This is volume the first of the three.
72561-sink-or-swim:
Sink or Swim, by the author of Recommended to Mercy, came out from Tinsley Brothers in 1868 in three volumes. This is the second. The contents are a fair map of its world, and its heroine's name is Honor.

What did Honor know, the first chapter asks. The colonel lays a plot, and gets his quietus by chapter six. Was Honor glad or sorry? Honor finds a new relation, and a grandmother's love shelters her. She shows a liking for the Bell, and feels like a lady. Lady Mill has business on hand, and Colonel Norcott feels paternal. John wishes the past undone, and decides against himself. Humble love and disappointment lead to the first step, in French in the contents, and silent sorrow. Sensation fiction judged its women harshly and read them hungrily; Honor is tried by every chapter heading.
72562-sink-or-swim:
Sink or Swim is a novel in three volumes by the author of Recommended to Mercy. The hosted copy is the third volume. It was printed at London by Tinsley Brothers in 1868. Twenty five chapters make up this last volume. The tale ends with a chapter called The Uses of Adversity and a Conclusion.

Honor Beacham stands on the brink of the abyss whose name is ruin. She has kept up a half deception about her father's condition. She hides it from her husband, whom she believes wrapped up in his own affairs. The chapter titles show the rest: John Beacham makes a discovery, John proves his right, John discovers his loss. Poor Sophy has her own chapter. The novel is a society tale of money, pride and marriage in the London season.
75013-jim:
A A Strachan wrote Jim, a tale of a former officer of the Canadian Mounted Police and his dog in the bush. Jim was a regimental dog, the teller confesses at the start. He had no use for anyone who did not wear a red tunic. He knew every bugle call as well as any trooper, the tale says.

When the bugler went to the parade ground, Jim followed punctiliously. He squatted and imitated the calls to his own satisfaction. At the dinner bugle he was always first at the mess room door. His day ended with Retreat as regularly as the sun went down. The teller took his discharge one April in the nineties and filed on a bush homestead north of the North Saskatchewan River. It nearly broke Jim's heart, he says. Only an old regimental tunic worn at intervals persuaded the dog to follow him.
77847-tim:
An anonymous novel titled Tim was published in London in 1891, first in October and reprinted in November that year. A verse from Second Samuel on love passing the love of women heads the book. The author dedicates it to a woman for whose entertainment it was first written. Her deathless memory receives the little book.

Tim's real name was not Tim, the narrator says, and he never asked what it was. The nickname came so early that no one remembered another. Tim was a slight, lean, brown child with regular features and a pale face. A nurse called him the thinnest and lightest baby ever seen. At seven he lives in an old house in a western county.
8080-a-passionate-pilgrim:
Henry James's early tale follows an American narrator who, intending to sail home in early June, spends six weeks in England instead. He lodges at an antique hostelry east of Temple Bar, in what he calls the Johnsonian quarter. And on his first evening descends to the little coffee-room to order dinner from the solitary waiter. From that inn, the story moves into English society, old houses, and the pilgrim's passionate search for roots.

The tale shows James already at work on his great theme: Americans meeting England, and finding both enchantment and disappointment. Its title signals the narrator's ardour, which the English world meets with reserve. For readers tracing James's development, it is a charming early story, and a good companion to his later international novels.
8124-woodrow-wilson-as-i-know-him:
Joseph P. Tumulty, Woodrow Wilson's private secretary, wrote this memoir of the president he served, dedicating it to his mother Alicia Tumulty. Tumulty draws on books by George Creel, Ray Stannard Baker, William E. Dodd, and others, alongside his own experience, to cover Wilson's work, the war, and the peace. The memoir presents Wilson from inside the White House, through the most turbulent scenes of his presidency.

The book's value is its closeness: Tumulty saw Wilson decide, hesitate, and persevere, and he defends his chief with loyalty and detail. Historians use it with care, since a secretary's memoir is also an argument. For readers of presidential history, it offers an intimate, partisan, and vivid portrait of Wilson as his closest aide knew him.
9067-robert-browning-how-to-know-him:
William Lyon Phelps, a professor of English at Yale, wrote this guide to Robert Browning and his poems. Phelps dedicates it to James Whitcomb Riley with affection and respect. Chapters take up the man, his theory of poetry, his lyrics, and his dramatic monologues. A full list of poems aids the reader.

Phelps walks through Abt Vogler, Andrea del Sarto, and Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came, among many others. He stresses Browning's optimism and his gift for voices. For new readers, this is a friendly door into a poet long thought hard to grasp.
9834-the-talleyrand-maxim:
J. S. Fletcher wrote The Talleyrand Maxim in 1920, a mystery of solicitors, wills, and a clerk bent on rising. Linford Pratt, senior clerk to Eldrick and Pascoe of Barford, desires to get on by hook or by crook, so long as crookedness stays safe. Death brings opportunity in chapter one, and terms, tricks, and a power of attorney follow. A woman in black and a telephone message deepen the case.

Pratt's schemes cross a shop-boy, fortunate possessors, and a headquarters conference, till cards lie on the table. Fletcher writes with brisk, legal suspense. A reader gets a taut postwar mystery, where a clerk's ambition becomes a crime.
a-passionate-pilgrim: Henry James follows an American visitor spending six weeks in England before sailing home, gathering impressions he has so far known only through reading. Lodging at an antique hostelry east of Temple Bar in London, he takes his dinner in the little coffee room of the Red Lion. The tale turns on what such a pilgrim sees, feels, and misunderstands when the motherland finally stands before his eyes.
britannica-1911-abu-l-qasim:
Abu-l-Qasim, known in Europe as Abulcasis, was an Arabian physician and surgeon who flourished at Cordova in the tenth century. The Britannica entry admits that no details of his life are known. He served as physician to the caliph 'Abdur-Rahman III, whose reign ran from 912 to 961, and his fame rests on books rather than biography.

Part of his medical compendium reached Latin readers in the sixteenth century, printed at Augsburg in 1519. His manual of surgery had the longer reach, printed at Venice in 1497 and at Basel in 1541. An Arabic and Latin edition prepared by John Channing appeared at Oxford in 1778, in two volumes.
britannica-1911-barrande-joachim:
Joachim Barrande (1799–1883) was an Austrian geologist and palaeontologist, a student of fossils. He was born at Saugues in France on 11 August 1799. He trained as an engineer at the École Polytechnique in Paris. His first post was tutor to the duc de Bordeaux, grandson of Charles X, and when the king abdicated in 1830 he followed the royal exiles to Prague.

Settled at Prague from 1831, Barrande turned from engineering works to the fossils of Bohemia's Lower Palaeozoic rocks. Murchison's Silurian System of 1839 spurred him to study the matching Bohemian strata. For ten years his hired collectors gathered upwards of 3,500 fossil species, trilobites above all. The first volume of his Système silurien du centre de la Bohême appeared in 1852, and twenty-one quarto volumes followed by 1881.
britannica-1911-basim:
Basim, a town of India in the Akola district of Berar, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands fifty-two miles south-south-east of Akola station on the Great Indian Peninsula railway, and its population in 1901 was 13,823. Until 1905 Basim was the headquarters of its own district, covering 2949 square miles. In that year the district was abolished and its taluks, its local subdivisions, were split between the districts of Akola and Yeotmal.

Land and farming fill the second half. The western part is a fertile tableland about 1000 feet up, sloping toward the rich Penganga valley. The east is low hills with poor grass, woodland stretches, and peaks near 2000 feet. The climate is praised as better than elsewhere in Berar, with cool night breezes after hot summer days. Crops were millet, wheat, other grains, pulse, oilseeds, and cotton, and the town had cotton ginning factories.
britannica-1911-becher-johann-joachim:
Johann Joachim Becher, a German chemist and man of schemes who lived from 1635 to 1682, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Spires, the son of a Lutheran pastor who died young. A stepfather wasted the small wealth of the house. At thirteen Becher had to feed himself, his mother, and his brothers.

He taught and learned trades by day and read all night. Books on metals, speech, and the deep earth poured from his pen. He pushed plans for mills, for trade monopolies, and for German colonies in Guiana. Such schemes made foes, and he fled Munich for fresh patrons. Mainz and Vienna took him in as doctor and as a guide on trade. His chief work of science treats of what lies beneath the earth.
britannica-1911-blenheim:
Blenheim is a village in Bavaria, Germany, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains why its name is known far beyond it. The village stands on the left bank of the Danube, about thirty miles north-east of Ulm, with some 700 people. On 13 August 1704 it saw a great battle.

The entry tells how French and Bavarian forces under Marshals Tallard and Marsin were beaten there by English and Austrian troops under Marlborough and Prince Eugene. In honor of that win, a grand house near Woodstock in England was built for Marlborough and named Blenheim Palace. The entry also sets out the ground of the fight, between the hills and the marshy Danube valley.
britannica-1911-cherubim:
Cherubim is the Hebrew plural of cherub, a word for imaginary winged animal figures of a sacred character. Scripture places them in Solomon's temple and on the ark of the tabernacle, as bearers of Yahweh's throne or guardians of his abode. In Genesis they guard Paradise, and a psalm speaks of Yahweh riding upon a cherub. The entry asks whether such figures were material temple images or beings of faith.

One line of argument links the cherub to the storm cloud and to a mythic bird, since Ezekiel joins his creatures to storm wind and bright cloud. Ezekiel gives his cherubim four faces, while another passage gives two. Winged bulls and lions with human faces in Babylon and Assyria offer a close parallel. Figures from north Syria and names tied to the god Rakab'el close the search for origins.
britannica-1911-coppee-francois-edouard-:
François Édouard Joachim Coppée (1842–1908) was a French poet and novelist born in Paris on 12 January 1842. His father held a small civil service post. His mother, by the entry's praise, gave him much by her care. He passed through the Lycée Saint-Louis and became a clerk in the war ministry. Verse brought him public favour as a poet of the young Parnassian school.

His first printed verses date from 1864. A gathered volume came in 1866, with more books close behind. In 1869 his first play, Le Passant, won marked praise at the Odéon. Short verse dramas of the war years won warm applause as well. He held a post in the senate library, then became archivist of the Comédie-Française in 1878. Election to the Academy in 1884 freed him from office for good. Verse kept coming from his pen after that.
britannica-1911-ettenheim:
Ettenheim is a German town in the grand-duchy of Baden, on the Ettenbach under the Black Forest's western slope. It lies 7 miles east of the Rhine by rail and had 3,106 people in 1900. Its Roman Catholic church holds ceiling frescoes and the tomb of Cardinal Rohan. Rohan, the last prince bishop of Strassburg, lived here from 1790 to 1803. A Protestant church and a medieval town-hall complete the chief buildings.

Tobacco, soap and leather are made, and wine and farm produce are traded. Eddo, bishop of Strassburg, founded the town in the 8th century. It stayed with that see until 1802, when it passed to Baden. The duke of Enghien, a refugee here since 1801, was arrested in the town on 15 March 1804. He was taken to Paris and shot on 20 March. The Benedictine abbey of Ettenheimmünster, founded in the 8th century, was dissolved in 1803.
britannica-1911-gandersheim:
The 1911 Britannica article on Gandersheim describes a town of Germany in the duchy of Brunswick. It stands in the deep valley of the Gande river. Its population was 2,847 in 1905. The town has two Protestant churches, a palace used as law courts, and the old abbey. It makes linen, cigars, beet sugar, and beer.

The account gives most space to the abbey. Duke Ludolf of Saxony founded it in 856. His daughter Hathumoda was its first abbess. The article follows the abbey's privileges and its imperial standing. It traces the line of Protestant abbesses down to 1803. It also recalls the town's literary memory. The poet Hroswitha belonged to the sisterhood. A rhyming chronicle by Eberhard is among the earliest works in low German.
britannica-1911-germersheim:
Germersheim is a walled town of Germany described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in Rhenish Bavaria, where the Queich meets the Rhine, south-west of Speyer. Its people numbered 5,914 in 1905. It holds two churches, a synagogue, a school, and a hospital. Its trades are fishing, ship building, and brewing.

The town stood as a Roman stronghold with the name of Vicus Julius. Its fort was rebuilt by the emperor Conrad the Second, but the town was founded in 1276 by Rudolph the First. He gave it the rights of a free city of the empire. From 1330 it formed part of the Palatinate of the Rhine. The French took and wasted it in 1674, and a war of succession for it ran to the peace of 1697. The French were beat there in 1744 and again in 1793. The new town was built in 1835.
britannica-1911-heppenheim:
Heppenheim is a town of Germany, in the grand-duchy of Hesse-Darmstadt, on the Bergstrasse between Darmstadt and Heidelberg, 21 m. N. of Heidelberg by rail. Its people numbered 6,364 in 1905. The parish church stands on the site of one said to have been built by Charlemagne about 805. The town also has a town hall of interest and several schools.

On a lone hill close by stand the wide ruins of Starkenburg castle, built by Abbot Ulrich von Lorsch about 1064 and destroyed in the Seven Years' War. Another hill, the Landberg, served as a place of assembly in the middle ages. Heppenheim first belonged to the abbey of Lorsch and became a town in 1318. It later passed to the Rhenish Palatinate and came to Hesse-Darmstadt in 1803. Hops, wine and tobacco are grown round it, and there are large stone quarries and several small trades in the town itself.
britannica-1911-hildesheim:
Hildesheim is a town and episcopal see of Germany, in Hanover, at the north foot of the Harz Mountains, on the Innerste, 18 m. S.E. of Hanover. Its people numbered 47,060 in 1905. Narrow, crooked streets hold many old houses with overhanging storeys and richly carved wooden fronts.

The cathedral, of the mid-11th century, is famed for Bishop Bernward's bronze doors, carved with reliefs from the stories of Adam and of Christ. It also holds a brazen font of the 13th century and a bronze column of 1022 with scenes from Christ's life. A rose-bush on the crypt wall is said to be a thousand years old. St Godehard's church and Bernward's St Michael add to the town's early art.
britannica-1911-hochheim: Hochheim is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on high ground near the right bank of the Main, three miles east of Mainz, with 3,779 people in 1905. The entry notes its two churches and its extensive trade in wine. The English word hock, the general term for Rhine wine, is derived from the town's name. Hochheim appears in chronicles as early as the seventh century.
britannica-1911-hohenheim:
Hohenheim is a village of Germany, in the kingdom of Württemberg, 7 m. S. of Stuttgart by rail. Its population is just 300. It came in 1768 from the counts of Hohenheim to the dukes of Württemberg. In 1785 Duke Karl Eugen built a country house there, with grounds.

That house is now the seat of the most important agricultural college in Germany. The college was founded in 1817 and raised to a high school in 1865. It now ranks as a technical high school with university status. The short entry thus joins a tiny village of 300 people to the country's leading school of agriculture, housed in a duke's country seat.
britannica-1911-jehoiakim:
Jehoiakim is a Bible history article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a king of Judah. His name means Yahweh raises up. He was a son of Josiah. When Josiah fell at Megiddo, the people chose his younger brother Jehoahaz as king. Pharaoh Necho then summoned that brother and carried him off to Egypt.

In his stead Necho set Eliakim on the throne and changed his name to Jehoiakim. For a time the new king paid heavy tribute to Egypt. Then the Chaldean empire rose under Nebuchadrezzar, and Egypt was crushed at Carchemish in 605 before Christ. After three years of loyalty, Jehoiakim revolted. Raids by Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites followed. The whole land fell into Nebuchadrezzar's hands by the close of the reign. The entry shows a small king caught between two great powers.
britannica-1911-jotunheim:
Jotunheim, or Jotun Fjelde, is a mountain region of southern Norway described in a 1911 Britannica article. It lies between Gudbrandsdal on the east and the head of the Sogne fjord on the west. Within an area of about 950 square miles stands the highest mountain in the Scandinavian Peninsula. That peak is Galdhöpiggen, at 8,399 feet.

Several other peaks fall but little short of it. Glittertind rises to 8,380 feet, and Memurutind to 7,966 feet. They face Galdhöpiggen across the Visdal valley. To the south, between lakes Gjende and Bygdin, stand more peaks over 7,000 feet. In the west rises Skagastölstind, the chief summit of the Horunger range. The upper parts of the main valleys have a character of their own, the text says. Mountain readers get the roof of Norway in one tight survey of peaks and lakes.
britannica-1911-leitrim:
Leitrim is a county of Ireland in the province of Connaught. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it about 613 square miles. The north is an elevated tableland with wild scenery. Truskmore, its highest ground, reaches 1,712 feet. The south is lower, level, and richly wooded. The coast on Donegal Bay runs only about three miles. The Shannon, flowing from Lough Allen, forms its south west border.

Lakes dot the county: Allen, Macnean, Scur, and Melvin among them. Lough Melvin is noted for its gillaroo trout. The floor of the county is mostly limestone rock. Sandstone shows at Lough Melvin and in the far south. Round Lough Allen the hills hold coal seams over clay ironstone. That ironstone gave Slieve Anierin, the iron mountain, its name. The entry then turns to the broken Silurian ground of the north.
britannica-1911-montefiore-sir-moses-hai:
Montefiore, Sir Moses Haim is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Jewish giver to good causes. He was born at Leghorn on the twenty-fourth of October 1784 and died in 1885. He was the eldest son of Joseph Elias Montefiore, a London merchant. His forebears were Jewish merchants who settled in Italy in the sixteen hundreds.

His grandfather crossed from Leghorn to London in 1758. The young Montefiore entered the Stock Exchange. His uncle paid twelve hundred pounds for his right to act as one of the twelve licensed Jewish brokers of the city of London. In 1812 he wed Judith Cohen, whose sister was the wife of Nathan Mayer Rothschild. That marriage tied him close in business to the great banking house. His own brother wed a Rothschild sister as well.
britannica-1911-parchim:
Parchim is a town of Germany in the grand duchy of Mecklenburg Schwerin, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It stands on the Elde, which flows through it in two arms. It lies 23 miles south east of Schwerin, on the rail line from Ludwigslust to Neubrandenburg. Its count in 1905 was 10,397 souls in the town.

Parchim was the birthplace of Moltke, to whom a monument was erected in 1876. It is an ancient place surrounded with walls in part. It contains a Gothic town hall and two churches of interest to visitors. Founded about 1210, it was for part of the 1300s the residence of one branch of the dukes of Mecklenburg. It became a prosperous industrial town in the 1500s, but that prosperity was destroyed by the Thirty Years War.
britannica-1911-pilgrim:
Pilgrim is a word traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a wanderer, most of all one who travels to a holy place. The first English forms came through French from a Latin word for a stranger or a foreigner. That Latin word in turn was built from words for through and for land, and meant one who has come from abroad.

It was the custom for pilgrims to bring back a badge as proof of their trip to a shrine. The badges were made of lead or pewter and bore a sign of the place. They are named in the Canterbury Tales and in Piers Plowman, and great stores of them, dredged from the Thames and the Seine, are kept in museums. The badges were worn pinned to the hat or the cape.
britannica-1911-ribeiro-bernardim:
Bernardim Ribeiro (1482-1552) is called the father of bucolic prose and verse in Portugal. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places his birth at Torrão in the Alemtejo. His father fled to Castile after a plot against King John II. The boy sheltered with kin near Cintra until a new king restored the family.

At court he won royal favor and a post as secretary. He studied law at Lisbon and joined the famed palace evening sessions of verse. There he worked beside Sá de Miranda and Cristovão Falcão. A blocked love for his cousin Joanna Zagalo, who was forced to wed another man, shadows the account.
britannica-1911-rouault-joachim:
Joachim Rouault is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rouault was a French soldier from an old family of Poitou. He attached himself to the dauphin, the future Louis the Eleventh. He rose to become the prince's premier squire, his first equerry.

The article follows his service in war after war. He marched against the Swiss in 1444 and fought the English in 1448. Posts followed: governor of Blaye and Fronsac, and constable of Bordeaux. At Castillon in 1453 he played a leading part in the victory that killed Talbot. He campaigned in Catalonia and became marshal of France in 1461. In 1471 he was made governor of Paris and defended Amiens and Beauvais. Late in life he fell from the king's favour and was sentenced, a fall the entry begins to recount.
britannica-1911-rudesheim:
Rudesheim is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a town in the Prussian Rhine province of Germany. It stands on the right bank of the Rhine, nineteen miles south west of Wiesbaden. Its population in 1905 was 4,773. The town sits at the lower end of the famed vineyard district of the Rheingau, opposite Bingen.

That setting, just above a romantic gorge of the river, makes it a favoured centre for tourists. Behind the town rises the Niederwald hill, crowned by a national monument to the war of 1870 and 1871. The entry lists old towers and castles in the town, one built in the thirteenth century for the archbishops of Mainz. A Gothic church holds paintings and monuments of note. Local work rests mainly on the making of wine.
britannica-1911-scrim: Scrim, a light open weave cloth, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is usually made of cotton or flax fibre. It is used in bookbinding, upholstery, and other industries of the day. It also serves as a backing to strengthen paper, as in maps and packing paper. Jute scrims are sometimes made for that purpose and treated to resist moisture. Some jute nets of this kind hold up the branches of fruit trees and keep birds from the fruit.
britannica-1911-urim-and-thummim:
Urim and Thummim, terms used in the Bible, are explained in a study entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They name one way the ancient Hebrews sought the will of God. Most scholars now agree the method was a kind of sacred lot. With dreams and the prophetic word, it formed a known channel for divine answers.

A passage in the first book of Samuel shows how the lot worked. Set questions put a plain choice, guilt or innocence, yes or no. Lots were cast in stages to narrow the answer down to one man. The rite was bound to the ephod and was the right of the priests alone. The Blessing of Moses gives the Urim and Thummim to the tribe of Levi. Like lots were cast among the Arabs before Islam, with marked arrow shafts that bore commands or bans.
britannica-1911-weinheim:
Weinheim, a town of Germany in the grand duchy of Baden, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Bergstrasse at the foot of the Odenwald hills. Heidelberg lies eleven miles to the south, on the rail line to Frankfurt. The census of 1905 counted 12,560 people there.

Ruins of the old town walls still ring part of Weinheim. Its chief buildings are a Gothic town hall and the ruined castle of Windeck. A modern castle of the counts of Berckheim and a house of the Teutonic Order also stand there. The town makes leather, machinery, and soap, and grows fruit and wine. Its mild air draws health seekers, and walkers use it as a base for the Odenwald. Chronicles name it as early as the eighth century, as a fief of Lorsch abbey. In the Thirty Years' War it was taken and plundered more than once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abarim: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abarim describes a mountain range across the Jordan, running south from Mount Nebo, perhaps reaching the Arabian desert. The Vulgate gives its meaning as passages. Its north end bore the name Phasga, or Pisgah, whose highest peak was Mount Nebo. Balaam blessed Israel a second time from Mount Phasga, Moses saw the Land of Promise from there, and Jeremias hid the ark there, according to the Second Book of Maccabees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-von-be:
Albert von Behaim, also known as Albertus Bohemus, was a papal partisan in the struggle with the Emperor Frederick II, born about 1180 near Passau and dead there in 1260. He went to Rome in 1205 and served at the papal court as a legal expert. In 1237 he returned to Germany and helped form a league against Frederick between the rulers of Bavaria, Bohemia, and Austria.

When Frederick was excommunicated in 1239, Behaim became permanent papal delegate. He pressed the sentence on Germany's bishops, excommunicating negligent clergy and laymen of rank when they failed him. His severity bore no fruit, and he had to leave the country, though he kept working against the emperor at the Council of Lyons in 1245. He ended his days at Passau, where he had been dean of the chapter since 1246, leaving two diaries known as the Missivbücher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-joseph-:
Anton Joseph Binterim, a German theologian born at Dusseldorf in 1779, served fifty years as parish priest of Bilk. After Franciscan training, he was ordained at Cologne in 1802, then left religious life when his monastery was suppressed. Appointed pastor of Bilk in 1805, he stayed until his death in 1855, writing tirelessly in defence of the church.

His treatises answered the rationalists of his day from ancient church and literary sources. He also fought Prussian law on mixed marriages, which stripped mothers of rights over their children's faith. Enemies accused him of intrigue with Rome, and he spent six months jailed at Wesel. The entry presents a combative pastor-scholar who never left his parish post.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnold-pannar:
Arnold Pannartz and Konrad Sweinheim, both printers, Pannartz dead about 1476 and Sweinheim in 1477, brought Gutenberg's invention to Italy. Pannartz was perhaps from Prague and Sweinheim from Eltville near Mainz, where Zedler believes Sweinheim worked with Gutenberg in 1461 to 1464. Whether Pannartz had joined Sweinheim in Germany is unknown, but together they carried printing south.

The Benedictine monastery of Subiaco became the cradle of Italian printing, probably at the summons of Cardinal Giovanni of Turrecremata, its commendatory abbot. They arrived in 1464, and their first Subiaco book, a Donatus grammar, has not survived. The first Italian printed book still extant is their Cicero, On the Orator, issued in September 1465, followed by Lactantius in October 1465 and Augustine's City of God in 1467.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baal-baalim:
Baal, plural Baalim, is a Semitic word meaning lord or owner. In Hebrew a man is called baal of a house, a field, cattle, wealth, and a wife. A ram is baal of two horns, and Joseph's brothers called him a baal of dreams. Inscriptions show the same broad use in other Semitic tongues. In the Hebrew Bible the plural keeps the singular's senses, though translations use it only for deities. The local Baals named are gods, not images.

As a god's name, Baal kept its sense of ownership and was qualified: Baal of Tyre, Harran, Tarsus, Hermon, Lebanon, Tamar, and heaven. Several Baals held titles, among them Baal of the Covenant in Judges. The article goes on to trace Baal worship, its emblems, and its place in Israel's religion. It draws on a source list from Movers to Smend. Its notes guide on the plural in Samuel and Kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cherubim:
An entry on the cherubim, angelic beings or their images, named often in the Old Testament and a single time in the New. The word cherub comes from the Assyrian kirubu, from a root meaning to be near, so cherubim are the near ones, the courtiers who surround God's majesty. The entry notes the word should be spoken qerub, with a hard sound.

In art, cherubim most often mean the sculpted, engraved, and embroidered figures that adorned the Jewish sanctuary. Two gold figures stood on the lid of the Ark, and Solomon set two huge olive-wood figures overlaid with gold in the Holy of Holies. Cherubim were also embroidered on the veil between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies and engraved as a motif, a repeated design, in wood and metal through the Temple. The entry weighs their forms and their place in worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dietrich-von-:
Dietrich von Nieheim, a German historian of the Middle Ages, was born between 1338 and 1340 in Paderborn's diocese. He took his name from the small town of Nieheim and spent years studying law in Italy. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him into the papal chancery at Avignon under Urban the Fifth, where he served as a notary. He went with Gregory the Eleventh back to Rome in 1377.

Dietrich is best known for his writings on the Western Schism, the split that set rival popes against each other. As abbreviator and later servant of the curia, he watched the crisis from inside. He died at Maastricht in 1418, leaving chronicles that historians still use to trace the schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elohim:
Elohim is the common Hebrew name for God. This entry weighs its form, its sense, and its roots. It is a plural form. Yet the usage of the language gives no support, the entry insists, to the idea that it preserves early polytheism or a blend with higher spirits. Grammarians call it a plural of majesty, rank, abstraction, or magnitude. The Ethiopic plural amlak likewise became a proper name for God.

Etymology divides scholars. Some take Elohim as the plural of Eloah, from a root meaning dread or seeking refuge. The name then first meant the object of dread. Others take it from El, with Eloah grown from a stem meaning mighty. The entry notes that forty-one of the fifty-seven uses of Eloah fall in Job. The rest fall in late or poetic texts. It tests each theory against the texts with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-gom:
Francisco Gomes de Amorim, born at Avelomar near Oporto on 13 August 1827 and dead on 4 November 1891, was a Portuguese poet, dramatist, and novelist of the Romantic age. His parents were respectable yet so poor that he left school at ten, went to Brazil, and worked in a business house at Para. There he studied the manners and dialects of Amazon Indian tribes. Returning to Portugal at twenty, he came under the spell of Almeida Garrett and the plan for a national drama.

Under the revolutionary ideas of 1848 he wrote poems on liberty, the fall of Hungary, and Garibaldi. His first play, Ghigi, performed at Lisbon in 1852 with signal success, began a long series of dramas, including Odio de raca, Aleijoes sociaes, Figados de tigre. A prohibicao, A viuva, A abnegacao, and Os herdeiros do millionario followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-jose:
Francois Joseph Heim, born near Belfort in 1787 and dead at Paris in 1865, was a French historical painter of early talent and long official honour. He began work at eight and won first prize for drawing at Strasburg before eleven. In 1803 his family sent him to Paris to study under Vincent, the best teaching they could afford. In 1807 he won an Academy prize with Theseus and the Minotaur and a travelling scholarship that took him to Rome.

Back in Paris he won the Academy's gold medal, became a full member in 1829 and professor in 1831. He was appointed painter to the Institute of France, exhibiting over sixty portraits of members whose drawings now hang in the Louvre. His historical and religious pictures were very attractive, the best being Jacob in Mesopotamia, painted in 1814 and now at Bordeaux.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-corn:
Renaissance figure Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim, born at Cologne in 1486, was by reputation knight, doctor, and magician, and he earned and repaid his conservative enemies' hatred across a wandering life. Student at Cologne and Paris, teacher of Hebrew at Dôle and in England, soldier under Maximilian who knighted him, he finished his Occult Philosophy, a blend of Neoplatonism and Cabala, about 1510.

Banished from Cologne for debt and dying poor at Grenoble or Lyons in 1534 or 1535, he left works steeped in occultism. They attacked scholasticism, relic veneration, canon law, and hierarchy while calling Scripture the philosopher's stone. Openly sympathetic to Luther's tone without joining him, he influenced Giordano Bruno. His 1527 book on the vanity of the sciences was translated across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hildesheim:
Hildesheim is a German diocese in Hanover east of the Weser, plus the duchy of Brunswick, founded under Emperor Louis the Pious. Legend says a miracle moved Louis to choose the present cathedral site over the village of Elze, where he built Germany's first chapel dedicated to the Mother of God. The founding date varies by account from 814 to 822, and the first bishop was Gunthar.

Rich gifts, immunities, and feudal sovereignty soon brought the see prosperity and power. Its brightest age came under Bishops Bernward, Godehard, and Hezilo in the eleventh century. Bernward's taste gave the cathedral its famous bronze doors, the Christ column, and the Bernward cross, plus the church of St. Michael, whose western crypt holds his tomb. Gandersheim Abbey also belonged to its orbit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-nico:
Johannes Nicolaus von Hontheim, writing as Justinus Febronius, was an auxiliary bishop of Trier whose book on the Church's constitution stirred a famous controversy. Born at Trier in 1701, he studied law and theology at Trier, Louvain, and Leyden, where the Gallican doctrines of Van Espen shaped him. Ordained in 1728, he became professor of the Pandects at Trier, then dean of St. Simeon, auxiliary bishop, and vicar-general.

In 1763 he published his treatise on the state of the Church and the lawful power of the Roman pontiff, arguing for limits on papal authority that became known as Febronianism. The book drew condemnation and long debate across Germany. Only two years before his death in 1790 did he renounce his doctrines with full sincerity. The entry paints him as short, energetic, hard-working, pious, and generous, yet faulted for spreading Gallican ideas in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-and-mich:
John Banim was an Irish poet, dramatist, and novelist whose work with his brother Michael aimed to do for Ireland what Scott had done for Scotland. Born at Kilkenny in 1798, he wrote verses and a tale by age ten, studied art at Dublin, and taught drawing on his return. A refused love ended in the girl's death and his own paralysis, leaving him a victim of spinal disease for life.

At twenty-three his tragedy Damon and Pythias staged at Covent Garden, Macready and Charles Kemble in the cast. With Michael he planned the Tales of the O'Hara Family, each brother revising the other's work so closely that their shares cannot be told apart. Moving to London in 1822, he poured out dramas, essays, and novels through constant pain, painting Irish character, brightly lit and deeply shadowed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konrad-sweynh:
Konrad Sweynheim, who died at Rome in 1477, was with Arnold Pannartz the first printer in Italy. Both clerics, they set up a press at Subiaco Abbey in 1464 at Cardinal Torquemada's invitation and moved it to Rome's Massimi Palace in 1467.

Their first books were a Donatus in 1464, then Cicero's De oratore and Lactantius in 1465. Between 1464 and 1472 they put out over 12,000 copies of thirty-seven works, mostly classics and Fathers, all by their own skill. Sweynheim, an engraver, likely cut dies, cast type, and set it, while Pannartz ran the press. He cut the first Greek type and first applied copper engraving to maps, with twenty-seven plates in the 1478 Ptolemy Cosmography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-langheim:
Langheim was a celebrated Cistercian abbey in Upper Franconia, Bavaria, in the Bamberg diocese. Three Bamberg brothers gave the estate to Bishop Otto. In 1132 he offered it to Ebrac's Cistercians, and Abbot Adam laid the foundation stone on 1 August 1132. The buildings were finished in 1142.

Under Abbot Adam, wisdom and holiness won bishops and nobles. Revenues grew, and parishes multiplied under the house. Ancient historians say it surpassed all monasteries in splendour and wealth, famed above all for generous hospitality. Disaster struck repeatedly. Bamberg's bishop seized property in 1385. Hussites burned it in 1429. Peasants torched it in 1535. Swedes pillaged it in 1632. Fire ended it on 7 May 1802, with secularization following in 1803.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-behaim:
Martin Behaim, or Martinus de Bohemia, was a German cartographer and navigator, born at Nuremberg in 1459 and dead at Lisbon in 1507. In 1481 or 1482 he went to Lisbon, where his fame as Regiomontanus's pupil won him a seat on John II's junta dos mathematicos, seeking better latitude methods.

He supplied the Jacob's staff and sun-declination tables, then sailed with Diego Cam along West Africa, reaching the Congo mouth and Walfisch Bay. Knighted in the Order of Christ in 1486, he married a daughter of Fayal and Pico governor Jobst von Hurter. At Nuremberg in 1492 he made his famous globe, the oldest surviving, about twenty-one inches across, marked only with equator, one meridian, tropics, and zodiac signs. His sway over Columbus and Magellan was once overstated and now stands in doubt, even his pupil claim and Cam voyage share questioned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrs-of-cu:
Martyrs of Cuncolim were five Jesuits killed at Cuncolim in Salcete, Goa, on Monday 25 July 1583. Fathers Rudolph Acquaviva, Alphonsus Pacheco, Peter Berno, and Anthony Francis, with lay brother Francis Aranha, met at Orlim church on 15 July. They marched to Cuncolim with some Christians to raise a cross and build a church.

Acquaviva was born at Atri in 1550, Pacheco of New Castile nobility about 1551, and Berno of humble Ascona parents in 1550. Francis was a poor Coimbra student born in 1553, and Aranha of wealthy Braga family about 1551. Their bodies were thrown into a well whose water Goa's people later sought for miraculous healing. Alongside the five, Goncalo Rodrigues, a Portuguese, and fourteen native Christians were also killed. The companions' cause was never brought before the archbishop of the time, nor since, for reasons now beyond judging. Their story rests on D'Souza's Oriente Conquistado and Goldie's Blessed Martyrs of Cuncolim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-micheas-of-ep:
