Micheas of Ephraim, also called Michas, takes his name from Hebrew Mikhayahu or Mikhayehu, shortened to Mikhah, meaning who is like Yahu. Judges 17-18 tells of a certain Michas, a hill-country Ephraimite who founded an idolatrous sanctuary. Having stolen 1,100 pieces of silver from his mother and restored them, he watched her devote 200 to making an idol, set up in his house.

Michas also made an ephod and teraphim. He first made his son priest, then hired a Bethlehem Levite, Jonathan, a descendant of Moses through Gershom. Danites on migration passed by, seized Jonathan and Michas's objects of idolatrous worship despite his protests, and set them up in the sanctuary they founded at Dan, named for themselves. The entry untangles the name's forms and follows the shrine from a household idol to a tribal sanctuary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-midrashim:
Midrashim is the term commonly given to ancient rabbinical commentaries on the Hebrew Scriptures. It is the plural of Midrash, a word found only twice in the Old Testament. In 2 Chronicles 13:22 and 24:27 the Vulgate renders it liber, book, and the Revised Version commentary. In rabbinical usage Midrash means study or exposition of Scripture in general.

Midrashim are, first, the free and often artificial explanations of the sacred text offered by its ancient expositors. Second, they are the collections of such explanations in commentary form. After the return from Babylon, the Law became the centre of Jewish religious life, and exposition flourished. The article traces the origins and kinds of midrashim, surveys the principal collections, and weighs their importance for understanding Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naim:
Naim, or Nain, is the city where Christ raised the widow's son to life, as Luke 7 relates. The Midrash gives the name the sense agreeable, for a place in Issachar in Galilee. Eusebius and Saint Jerome place Naim south of Mount Thabor, not far from Endor. Today, opposite Thabor and a mile and a half north of Endur, lies a village called Nain, meaning pleasantness.

It sits on the northwestern ridge of Jebel Dahy, the Little Hermon, commanding a magnificent view, with ruins beyond its boundary but no sign of fortifications. The gate of the city in Luke's story may have belonged to an enclosure wall against marauding tribes. A steep path climbs past an ancient church turned mosque, bought in ruins by Franciscans in 1880, who raised a chapel there, near Jewish rock-tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piligrim:
Piligrim was the tenth-century bishop of Passau remembered both for forging documents and for earnest missionary work. He was educated at the Benedictine monastery of Niederaltaich and made bishop in 971. He is credited with the Forgeries of Lorch, papal bulls fabricated to prove Passau the heir of an older archdiocese of Lorch.

By these papers he sought elevation to archbishop, the revival of dioceses in Pannonia and Moesia, and the pallium, a woollen band marking archiepiscopal rank, for himself. Apart from the forgeries, common enough in his age, he converted many pagans in Hungary, built schools and churches, and restored Benedictine rule at Niederaltaich before his death in 991.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-purim:
Purim, the Jewish feast whose name scholars dispute, gets a compact history here. Some derive the name from the Persian word for lot, or for full; others from an Aramaic root meaning to break into pieces. The feast recalls the deliverance of the Jews from Haman, minister of Xerxes, who won a royal edict for their extermination. The date of the massacre, 13 Adar, was fixed by lot, as the Book of Esther records.

Through the pleading of Esther, Jewess and queen, the edict was recalled. On 13 Adar the Jews, sure of royal protection, defended themselves and slew many of their enemies. In Susa, then the Persian capital, vengeance ruled for two days; elsewhere it lasted one day. Hence Purim falls on 15 Adar in Susa and on 14 Adar in other places. Reuss, Oppert, Vigouroux and Schürer supply the entry's critical sources on the feast and its story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolf-of-rud:
Rudolf of Rüdesheim, Bishop of Breslau, was born about 1402 and died at Breslau in January 1482. From 1422 to 1426 he studied at Heidelberg, graduating as master, then took a doctorate in ecclesiastical law in Italy and became auditor of the Rota. Numerous benefices came to him early, particularly in Mainz and Worms. From 1438 he represented Worms at the schismatic Council of Basle, befriending Enea Silvio de' Piccolomini, later Pius II.

Pius II, Paul II, and Emperor Frederick III entrusted Rudolf with important missions. Pius II named him Bishop of Lavant in Tyrol in 1463. Breslau came to him in 1468, when its people resisted their ruler George Podiebrad of Bohemia. The resulting war ended, with Rudolf's cooperation, in the Peace of Olmutz in 1479. Turning to his diocese's welfare, he sought to heal war's wounds and stress clergy's theological training.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seraphim:
Seraphim, a Hebrew plural, names a special class of heavenly attendants at Yahweh's court. Scripture mentions them distinctly only in Isaiah's account of his call, in chapter 6. This entry unfolds that vision. In the Temple, Isaiah saw Yahweh enthroned in glory, with mysterious guardians standing on each side. Each had six wings. Two bore them up, two veiled their faces, and two covered their feet, left bare as befitted priestly service.

The guardians called to one another, holy, holy, holy, Yahweh of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory. One flew to Isaiah with a live coal from the altar and touched his lips, cleansing them for inspired speech. Though pictured in human form with faces, hands, and feet, the seraphim remain shadowy figures, and the entry draws from the vision all that Scripture discloses about them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-joachim:
Joachim, father of Mary, rests on tradition the entry treats with open-eyed caution. His name means Yahweh prepares. Peter Damian warned that prying into matters evangelists left untold, above all Mary's parents, was blameable, needless curiosity. Yet tradition, grounded on very old testimonies, early hailed Joachim and Anne as parents of God's mother. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 traces that tradition to apocryphal gospels.

The Gospel of James, the Gospel of Mary's Nativity, and Pseudo-Matthew's Book of Mary's Nativity and the Saviour's Childhood supply the ultimate source, and their origin rightly rouses suspicion. Rejection from the canon and ungenuineness, the entry insists, do not mean no heed at all should be paid to some assertions. Beside much that is unworthy, genuine memories may survive. The entry thus holds tradition and criticism in balance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tschiderer-zu:
Johann Nepomuk Tschiderer zu Gleifheim, Bishop of Trent, born at Bozen on 15 February 1777 and died at Trent on 3 December 1860. His family had come from the Grisons to the Tyrol in 1529 and received a patent of nobility from Ferdinand III in 1620. He was ordained priest in 1800 by Bishop Emmanuel von Thun.

After parish work and teaching moral and pastoral theology at Trent, he served at Sarnthal from 1810 and Meran from 1819. He won a lasting name for zeal and charity. Made cathedral canon in 1826 and Bishop of Heliopolis in 1832, he became Prince-Bishop of Trent in 1834. He ruled twenty-five years in great simplicity, while spending freely on his cathedral and churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urim-and-thum:
Urim and Thummim were the sacred lot by which the ancient Hebrews sought signs of the divine will. Two other channels of divine speech were recognized: dreams and prophetic utterance. All three appear together in 1 Samuel 28:6, where Saul consults the Lord and receives no answer by dreams, by priests, or by prophets. The entry argues that the Douay rendering of priests there is wrong, resting on a mistaken Latin reading.

The words' sense, by Masoretic pointing, is plain enough: Urim comes from the Hebrew for light, or giving light, and Thummim from completeness or perfection. The entry discusses how the lot was kept, how it was consulted, and what scholars have guessed about its form, separating what Scripture says from later fancy. It offers a careful guide to a small but famous piece of Israel's worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-windesheim:
Windesheim was an Augustinian monastery near Zwolle whose congregation led Catholic reform in Holland and Germany before the Reformation. An offshoot of the Brethren of the Common Life, it answered mendicant attacks on the Brethren. On his deathbed in 1384 Gerard Groot urged some brethren to adopt an approved order's rule. His successor Florence Radewyns sent six chosen men, including Thomas à Kempis's elder brother John, to Eymsteyn to learn Augustinian ways.

In 1386 the six raised temporary huts at Windesheim, and in March 1387 began monastery and church, consecrated that October by Hubert Lebene, titular Bishop of Hippo. Under second prior Johann Vos, from 1391 to 1424, numbers swelled and foundations multiplied, Marienborn and Niewlicht in 1392 first among them. Boniface IX approved the chapter in 1395, and Martin V approved its constitutions at Constance. By 1407 it counted twelve houses, joined by seven Brabant houses in 1413 and twelve Neuss houses in 1430.
doe-osti-2996974-modeling-detonation-wit:
David Torres simulates a sheet explosive striking a tantalum plate, in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-29673, issued 29 September 2025. CartaBlanca is the laboratory's code for violent multi-material events on unstructured grids. Simulations can reveal flow and damage patterns that cameras and gauges cannot capture in the microseconds of a detonation.

Runs used the material point method, which carries material on moving points through a fixed grid. Mesh cells of 0.1, 0.05, and 0.025 cubic centimeters were compared at two microseconds after impact, with the explosive jetting at 700,000 centimeters per second. Speed and stress values shifted with mesh size, suggesting finer grids are needed. A discontinuous Galerkin method is flagged as the next step for the expanding gas phase.
doe-osti-3022914-resonance-self-shieldin:
LLNL report LLNL-TR-2011238, by Dermott Cullen, is a long argument for taking resonance self-shielding seriously in neutron transport calculations. Inside a resonance, neutrons at exactly the energies a nucleus absorbs best are depleted first. The flux dips where the cross section peaks. Treating cross sections as if the flux were smooth can badly misstate reaction rates in reactors and shielding.

The report backs the argument with worked Monte Carlo tallies. In its example problem the effective multiplication factor lands at 0.998986. The reaction balance is broken out channel by channel. Fission produces most new neutrons, and capture on the (n,gamma) channel takes the largest removal share. The elastic and inelastic scattering counts run to dozens of events per source neutron. Tables like these show how sensitive the whole balance is to resonance treatment, which is the author's point.
doe-osti-3024577-shoteam-superalloy-heat:
Timothy S Fisher of the University of California, Los Angeles, closes award DE-AR0001131, which ran September 2019 to June 2024, in a report dated December 22, 2025. SHOTEAM built superalloy heat exchangers for temperature extremes, aimed at ultra-high efficiency hybrid aviation power cycles. The unit targeted 50 kilowatts of thermal duty with supercritical carbon dioxide at 80 bar on the hot stream and 250 bar on the cold stream.

The hot stream enters at 800 degrees Celsius, so the design is a microtube shell-and-tube exchanger in a high-strength superalloy, supplemented with 3D-printed tube augmentations. Testing tracked oxidation of subscale tubes, creep behavior of Haynes 282 in standard and additive forms, reported in June 2023, and thermophysical property measurements. Front-page figures also list corner conditions such as 702 degrees at 245 bar.
doe-osti-3365374-resstock-measure-docume:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5500-96413, by Philip White and Andrew Parker, documents the cold climate air-source heat pump measure in ResStock 2025 Release 1. Cold climate heat pumps keep heating efficiently in deep winter, where older models gave up to backup resistance heat. ResStock modelers need exact rules for when a simulated home receives one.

Applicability logic turns on ducts and shared systems. Homes sharing an HVAC system qualify only in defined cases, such as a shared system serving central air conditioning. The reason is practical: installers need outdoor space for the condenser. One side effect gets flagged honestly: homes only partly cooled today become fully cooled by the upgrade, which can raise their cooling energy use. Compressor speed and the HSPF2 and SEER2 rating systems are specified for the measure.
doe-osti-3367035-user-manual-hydragnn-v5:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory manual ORNL/TM-2026/4590 documents HydraGNN version 5.0, the lab's distributed graph neural network code for materials and chemistry prediction. Massimiliano Lupo Pasini leads a nine-author team. Graph networks treat atoms as nodes and bonds as edges, learning properties from structure; HydraGNN trains one model on many tasks and datasets at once, across supercomputer nodes.

The manual tours the code's modules, from data loaders to the test suite. Example folders cover interatomic potentials, ultraviolet spectrum prediction, hyperparameter optimization, and model parallelism for foundation models. Non-chemistry examples include optimal power flow and Ising spin configurations. Version 5.0's distributed implementation targets the exascale machines at Oak Ridge, and the manual is the entry point for new users.
doe-osti-3367366-intelligent-experiments: A short Georgia Tech progress summary, two pages of text, reports on real-time AI for the sPHENIX heavy-ion experiment and the future Electron-Ion Collider, from Davendra Maharaj's team. One thread built a clustering pipeline for ALPIDE pixel sensors on field-programmable gate arrays, grouping hits by column pairs and stitching clusters across five streamed stages. A second ported connected-component analysis to the same hardware, reaching 14.8 times the CPU speed at 1.58 microseconds per graph. The document is a compact annual summary, not a full report.
doe-osti-3374531-overcoming-challenges-t:
INL/RPT-25-87321, an Idaho National Laboratory report, dated September 2025, takes up the roadblocks facing nuclear power at sea. The authors are Sanjay Haresh Mukhi and Marvin W. Fielding of the lab. Domenic Carlucci of the American Bureau of Shipping joins them. The study grew out of a Department of Energy funding call on fast-tracking commercial maritime demonstration projects.

Cost leads the list of hurdles. Setting up tests, building reactors, and creating port support all cost more than rival energy sources. A fission plant also needs extra safety systems, tighter quality rules, and more upkeep. Those steps guard the public, but they raise the bill. The authors warn that without full life-cycle cost studies, high start-up costs alone may scare off investors.
doe-osti-3379140-web-accessible-sorption:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory interim progress report LLNL-TR-2020711, by M. Zavarin and dated August 19, 2026, reports on a web-based sorption database for the nuclear waste repository program. The milestone number is M4SF-26LL010204053, under crystalline host rock research. Sorption is how strongly dissolved substances stick to mineral surfaces. It is a key input when modeling how a repository would contain waste over time.

The database, called L-SCIE, holds sorption data for bentonite backfill and crystalline host rock. It includes the high-temperature data a deep repository scenario needs. In 2025 it was rebuilt from a Microsoft Access file into an open MariaDB database. The report describes the new web interface for pulling data for performance assessment. It applies the tool to modeling a shale repository, and it lists proposed fiscal 2027 work.
doe-osti-3401580-intelligent-experiments:
Massachusetts Institute of Technology's final report for award DE-SC0022340, issued May 2026, closes Intelligent Experiments Through Real-time AI. The project worked on fast data processing and autonomous detector control for the sPHENIX experiment and future Electron-Ion Collider detectors. Gunther Roland, co-spokesperson of sPHENIX, was principal investigator. The reporting period ran from September 2023 to May 2026. Contributing authors include Cameron Dean, Hannah Bossi, and Philip Harris.

Four tasks structure the accomplishments. Physics simulation and offline data processing came first. Heavy-flavor tagging with machine learning followed, teaching algorithms to spot the rare decays physicists prize. The third task translated machine learning models into FPGA firmware with the hls4ml tool. Decisions could therefore run inside the detector's data stream in real time. A demonstrator implementation tied the pieces together. The report ends with the grant's status and outlook.
doe-osti-3452149-the-radioisotope-power-:
Oak Ridge manual ORNL/TM-2019/1249 Revision 1, dated August 2026, teaches use of RPS-DET version 2.0, a dose estimation tool for radioisotope power systems. Michael B. R. Smith, Douglas E. Peplow, Robert A. Lefebvre, and co-authors revised the manual. Space missions use such power systems far from the Sun.

Users can end a run by particle count or by run time. Toggles switch between the two stopping rules. An option saves neutron and photon flux by voxel, the small cubes of the 3D model. Mission safety staff can compute dose fields around a power source before hardware ships.
george-leatrim:
George Leatrim, or The Mother's Test, by Susanna Moodie, opens as a story told between friends. One lady calls it the most terrible instance of dishonesty she ever knew, in her own family's branches. Dr Leatrim, the subject, preaches at Westcliff. He is eloquent in the pulpit and solitary out of it. Some great domestic calamity, people say, weaned him from the world. Since his wife and only son died, no one has seen him smile.

Benevolence breathes from his sermons, his friend protests, from so austere a man. Moodie, the Canadian pioneer author of Roughing It in the Bush, wrote this tale of an English clergyman's hidden wound. The mother's test of the subtitle is the story's engine. A reputation for austere goodness is the mask. Behind it sits a theft, a sacrifice, and a mother's terrible arithmetic of love.
gerhard-the-coming-creed-of-the-world-is:
Frederick Gerhard published his plea for a new world faith at Philadelphia in 1884. Its motto is God is Love, taken from the first letter of John. In his preface Gerhard says his target is not the teaching of Jesus, which he calls sublime, but the dogma and priestcraft that he thinks have spoiled it. He calls the book the fruit of many years of thought.

Gerhard argues that creeds divide people, while love can unite them. He draws a sharp line between Christianity as a system and religion as a life of love. He urges readers to prove all things and hold fast to truth, in Paul's words. The book is a bold, earnest sample of free religious thought in America, written in a warm and urgent voice.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BishopJim_Bisho:
Jim Bishop was the journalist who turned single days into bestsellers: The Day Lincoln Was Shot, The Day Christ Died, and The Day Kennedy Was Shot. This magazine profile looks at the man behind that formula.

Bishop rebuilt famous days hour by hour from documents and interviews, and readers bought his books by the million. His Kennedy volume appeared in 1968 and carried his method to the assassination that defines this archive. A profile in a researcher's files shows the attention paid to the popular historians who shaped how America pictured November 22, 1963.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAJim_CIA_Jim:
A man identified only as 'Jim,' a former CIA contract agent, told a radio interviewer that the CIA was responsible for a massacre in the Congo. United Press International carried the report, drawn from his interview with Art Kevin of station KMPC.

Such claims surfaced through the 1960s and 1970s, as contract men from the Congo wars talked to journalists and the agency declined to answer. A wire report is the thinnest form of the story: the claim, the claimant's first name, and no adjudication. It is preserved as it moved on the wire, a fragment of the Congo's long and contested record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HoughtonJim_Hou: Harold Weisberg wrote on November 27, 2004 to Tony Marro of Newsday about Jim Hougan's book Secret Agenda. Weisberg, then in his nineties, was still arguing the cases of his life in letters to journalists. The surviving record gives the date, the recipient, and the book under discussion, but not the letter's arguments, so it stands as very late Weisberg correspondence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McNicholasJim_M: nsia-McNicholasJim McNicholas Jim: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TurnerJim_Turne: FBI agents interviewed Jim Turner, television director at WBAP-TV in Fort Worth, on July 22, 1964. The subject was his station's coverage of Lee Harvey Oswald's transfer, the event during which Jack Ruby shot Oswald on live television. Broadcasters were witnesses as well as reporters that weekend. The interview records what a man who helped put those pictures on air told the bureau.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Al:
Allende and Chile: Bring Him Down appeared in November 2020, days after the fiftieth anniversary of Salvador Allende's history-changing election as president of Chile. Its title quotes the spirit of Washington's orders toward his elected government.

The briefing book publishes records of the American campaign against Allende: money for opponents, propaganda, and economic pressure meant to make Chile's economy scream, as President Nixon put it. Released half a century on, the documents still carry force, because the campaign worked and a coup followed in 1973. For readers of that coup, the collection supplies the prequel in the plotters' own files.
jimgrim:
Jimgrim is an adventure novel by Talbot Mundy, published in 1922. Its contents page shows a long tale in two parts and twenty chapters. Part one is called The Reincarnated. Part two is called Messiah of Tinsel. Chapter titles speak in riddles and half-quoted lines. One offers to take a case, and another toys with crowning Jimgrim emperor.

Several chapters turn on a figure named Dorje, styled the Daring and the King of the World. One chapter asks for the key to Dorje's cipher, and another prints a long string of numbers. A woman claims to be the Queen of Sheba and says Jimgrim's name was stolen. Mundy's chapter list promises secret identities, codes, and intrigue around his hero Jimgrim.
markheim:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this short tale of a murder on Christmas Day, and it came out in 1885. It was first bound in his set The Merry Men, from which this text is drawn. Stevenson had a rare gift for the dark side of the soul in a brief tale.

Markheim, a dealer in old goods, kills a shop man for cash on the holy day. A strange guest then steps in, who may be the devil, or the man's own soul made plain. The talk that comes next probes guilt and grace with a force few short tales match.
more-goops-and-how-not-to-be-them-a-manu:
Gelett Burgess wrote this manual of manners for impolite infants as a sequel to his Goops book. Frederick A. Stokes published it at New York with ninety illustrations by the author. The Goops are naughty, thoughtless children shown in comic verse. Each picture and rhyme displays a fault for young readers to avoid.

Burgess, a San Francisco humorist, first made the Goops famous in magazines. The catalog pages list his nonsense books and lively city fairy tales. Parents bought the Goops books to teach table manners, cleanliness, and kindness by laughter. The sequel's subtitle promises the characteristics of many naughty children, depicted so that polite infants will not copy them.
nasa-tm-19660018727-irradiation-system-f:
F A Haley and R R Wyer at Lewis Research Center described an irradiation system for very cold experiments. The system works inside the Plum Brook Reactor. Their paper was prepared for a May 1966 meeting in California. Cryogenic work studies matter at extremely low temperatures. Doing it inside a reactor adds radiation to the cold. Their system lets samples sit in both conditions at once, under control.

Such combined tests serve reactor and space research alike. Materials in space face cold and radiation together, not one at a time. A purpose-built system makes the pair testable on the ground. The paper was offered for a symposium on irradiation capsule technology, where specialists traded designs for exactly this kind of rig.
nasa-tm-19720002890-target-contrast-cons:
A Mayer of the Ames Research Center wrote this August 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,082. It sets target signal needs for aircraft navigation systems that see by heat radiation. A radiometric receiver maps the faint power radiated by terrain below. It can also map beacons placed on the ground. Either map could guide an aircraft in poor visibility.

Mayer focused on waves near eight millimeters long. At chosen bands, such waves cross the air with little loss, even in extreme weather. Hardware for that size was available and compact. The small wavelength also promised sharp images. Those traits made all weather navigation by radiometry look practical.
nasa-tm-19720004689-thermal-coefficients:
Robert F. Mueller of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in October 1971, numbered X-644-71-418, on how fast nature absorbs the effects of technology. Recovery processes set that pace: plants regrowing, soil rebuilding, and pollution being cleansed from land and water. Mueller estimated thermal coefficients, heat-based rates, for these assimilation processes.

His estimates indicate that such processes run far more slowly in Earth's cold regions than in temperate ones. The difference runs from ten times to several hundred times. Cold-region environments are fragile largely because temperature limits the biological activity that repairs damage. The processes include vegetation growth, soil humus formation, and the work of microorganisms, plus chemical decay of wastes. Mueller suggests these uneven rates are important data when planning technological expansion in Arctic regions.
nasa-tm-19720005298-analysis-of-heat-tra:
Herbert J Gladden, Daniel J Gauntner, and John N B Livingood of the Lewis Research Center analyzed these vane cooling tests in December 1971, as NASA TM X-2376. The test piece was a turbine vane cooled three ways at once. Jets struck its inner wall, air scrubbed its passages, and a film of air coated its outer skin. The vane sat in a still cascade of similar blades for the tests.

Gas in the cascade reached very high heat and pressure. The catalog record gives peak values near twenty five hundred degrees Fahrenheit. The team gathered flow and heat transfer data throughout the runs. Average and local metal temperatures were matched in several ways. Turbine designers used such results to keep blades alive.
nasa-tm-19720010255-application-of-the-s:
Bobby G Junkin of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on December 10, 1971, as NASA TM X-64636. He worked in the Computation Laboratory there. The report applies the steepest ascent method to a reentry trajectory problem. Steepest ascent is a step by step way to improve a flight path. Each step nudges the controls toward the best payoff while respecting limits.

Junkin presents the direct optimization method in full detail. Starting control values enter as inputs to the process. Small test changes are then made to those controls. The method predicts, to first order, how payoff and constraint values will shift. Designers can then choose the most promising change. The approach served trajectory planning for returning spacecraft.
piccadilly-jim:
P. G. Wodehouse opens Piccadilly Jim at the Riverside Drive mansion of Mr. Peter Pett, financier. The house, he says, jumps out and bites at you, resembling in equal proportions a cathedral, a suburban villa, a hotel, and a Chinese pagoda. Mr. Pett wanders it like a lost spirit, hunting a quiet spot for his Sunday paper.

Since his marriage two years before, the place has filled with intruders, for Mrs. Pett writes voluminously and loves to be noticed. The novel's hero is her stepson Jim Crocker, the wild Piccadilly Jim of the title. Wodehouse builds farce from money, family, and mistaken identity on two continents.
robert-browning-how-to-know-him:
William Lyon Phelps, Lampson Professor of English Literature at Yale, wrote this guide to Robert Browning, with a portrait of the poet. He dedicates it to James Whitcomb Riley with sincere affection and respect. Seven chapters form the plan, from The Man to Browning's Optimism.

Chapters between treat Browning's theory of poetry, his lyrics, and his dramatic lyrics in turn. The dramatic monologues, his most famed form, get a chapter of their own. Poems of Paradox follows, asking how his strange tales serve his faith in life. A list of poems at the front runs from Abt Vogler and Andrea del Sarto to The Bishop Orders His Tomb.
robert-burns-how-to-know-him:
William Allan Neilson, professor of English at Harvard University, wrote this guide to Robert Burns, issued by Bobbs-Merrill of Indianapolis with copyright of 1917. A portrait by Nasmyth fronts the book, and Neilson dedicates it to his brother. He had also written Essentials of Poetry.

A list of poems with their page numbers shows the book's method: to know Burns through the poems themselves. Address to the Deil and Address to the Unco Guid stand among the first entries. Ae Fond Kiss, Afton Water, and Auld Lang Syne follow, with The Auld Farmer's New-Year Morning Salutation and The Bard's Epitaph. Songs and satires alike are set out for study.
sundown-slim:
Henry Herbert Knibbs wrote Sundown Slim, copyrighted in 1915 and printed at New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with illustrations by Anton Fischer. The western novel is dedicated to Everett E. Haraszthy, and its chapters stay in Arizona country throughout.

The contents open with Sundown in Antelope, run through The Joke and Thirty Miles to the Concho, and follow the canon trail to a place called The Last Chance. Later chapters bring a storm, a gift, and Sundown working as a vaquero. Knibbs was a poet of the range as well as a novelist. He writes of a wandering cowboy here. The man's soft heart and tall frame carry him far. He moves through scrapes, friendships, and range work under desert skies.
t-de-witt-talmage-as-i-knew-him:
T. De Witt Talmage As I Knew Him, printed at New York by E. P. Dutton and Company in 1912, is the famous preacher's own account of his life, finished after his death with concluding chapters by Mrs. T. De Witt Talmage. The contents mark the life off in seventeen milestones, with a biographical sketch of his last milestones added.

The illustrations show Talmage's parents, David and Catherine Talmage. They show his first church at Belleville, New Jersey. They show his service as chaplain of the Thirteenth Regiment of New York. They show the third Brooklyn Tabernacle too. That was the great church he filled for years. Talmage was among the most widely read sermon writers of his century, and the book tells his rise in his own hearty, anecdotal voice.
the-dozen-from-lakerim:
Rupert Hughes's The Dozen from Lakerim, dated 1899, tells of life at a boys' academy. Hughes notes that about half ran first in St. Nicholas magazine, and begs pardon for slighting books and studies in favour of games and pranks between classes. The book is set in memory of his father, and pictures by C. M. Relyea fill its list of plates.

Twelve schoolmates, the Lakerim club, fill the tales with sport and scrapes. Scenes name a cross-country run, a boxing match, and boys tied in sacks. Hughes writes school life as play first.
the-honorable-peter-stirling-and-what-pe: Paul Leicester Ford wrote The Honorable Peter Stirling and What People Thought of Him, dated 1894, with Stitt Publishing Company and Henry Holt & Co. named on the title page. A table of contents lists thirty-three chapters, numbered in Roman numerals with no titles given for any of them. Only the title page and contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear, and no plot beyond the title's promise can be stated from what is shown.
the-passionate-pilgrim:
William Shakespeare's The Passionate Pilgrim is a group of poems on love, printed here under numbered headings. The first poem begins with a lover whose mistress swears she is made of truth. He says he believes her, though he knows she lies, so that she may think him a simple youth. Both hide their age, since love's best habit is a soothing tongue.

The second poem speaks of two loves, one of comfort and one of despair. A fair man is the poet's better angel, and a dark woman his worser spirit, who tempts the angel from his side. The third poem turns to a woman's eye and a broken vow. Doubt and jealousy run through the set.
the-talleyrand-maxim: J. S. Fletcher's Talleyrand Maxim is dated 1920, and this record gives its title page and chapter list without any of the novel itself. Seventeen chapters are named, starting with Death Brings Opportunity and moving through In Trust, The Shop-Boy, The Fortunate Possessors, and Point-Blank. Later headings mention a power of attorney, a first trick, and cards laid on the table. The skeleton suggests a mystery of money, trust, and scheming, though Fletcher's plotting and his characters stay beyond the pages present.
woodrow-wilson-as-i-know-him:
Joseph P. Tumulty, Wilson's White House aide, wrote this personal portrait of President Woodrow Wilson. His preface warns that Wilson disliked being written about. Friends were expected to stay silent while foes talked. Tumulty tells of a 1920 speech in Bethesda that cooled Wilson's manner for days. Wilson never read the speech, Tumulty believes.

Tumulty still wrote the volume from long daily contact. He drew on Wilson's public addresses and on many earlier books. Readers get an insider's view of Wilson's habits, pride, and reserve. Loyalty and candour mix in the telling, since Tumulty knew his subject might never open the volume.
